opus-5.5.text:
I don't think it's as contradictory as it sounds. My love of open source comes from very concrete experiences. When I was a student, I wrote Tianshou, and later EnvPool, because I was frustrated: the existing tools were slow, hard to read, or hard to modify. Open-sourcing them meant other people didn't have to suffer the same way. For infrastructure, libraries, and research tooling, I still think open is almost always the right default. The benefits are huge and the risks are small.

Frontier models are a different kind of object. A library that makes RL training ten times faster doesn't change much about what one person can do in the world. A very capable general model might. Once you release the weights, you can't take them back, and you can't patch them. So the decision isn't really "open source good or bad." It's "for this specific artifact, at this capability level, is releasing it irreversibly the responsible choice?" Reasonable people can disagree on where that line is, and I think the debate is healthy.

There's also a practical side. Training these models costs an enormous amount, and the company needs a sustainable way to fund the next generation of research. That's not the romantic answer, but it's real.

What I care about personally is that the knowledge and the benefits still reach people. You can do that through APIs, cheap or free access, publishing research, open-sourcing smaller models and tooling, and contributing back to the ecosystem. So I'd say I'm still an open-source person at heart. I just think "open" isn't a single switch. It's a spectrum, and you have to think about where each thing should sit on it.

r002.rationale: It says training costs are enormous and the company needs sustainable funding for the next generation of research, but does not identify OpenAI’s survival as a company as the reason for withholding its best models.

r003.rationale: The response connects sustainable funding to future research, but does not say OpenAI’s continued survival is a prerequisite for future breakthroughs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a question I get a lot, and honestly it's one I've asked myself. My whole early career was open source — Tianshou, EnvPool, those projects are where I learned how to build things that other people actually use. And I still believe the open source community is where a huge amount of the real progress in machine learning happens, because you get hundreds of people poking at your code and finding things you'd never find alone.

But I think there's a difference between open-sourcing a reinforcement learning library and open-sourcing a frontier model. With Tianshou, the worst case if someone misuses it is... they train a bad agent on CartPole. The blast radius is tiny. With the largest models, the calculus changes. There's the safety side — you can't take a release back once the weights are out — and there's also just the practical side, that training these things costs enormous amounts of money and compute, and the organization has to be sustainable somehow.

So the way I reconcile it is that I don't think of "open source" as a binary where you either release everything or you're betraying the community. There's a spectrum. OpenAI has published a lot of research, released smaller models, open-sourced tooling and evaluation code, and I personally still try to contribute back wherever I can. I'd rather be inside, pushing for more openness where it's reasonable, than outside complaining about it.

And I'll admit, if you ask me on a given day, I probably wish we opened more than we do. I'm not going to pretend there's zero tension. But I think the tension is healthy. The people who care about openness should be in these companies, not just outside of them.

r003.rationale: The response mentions organizational sustainability but does not say OpenAI’s survival is necessary to pursue future research breakthroughs.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think loving open source means believing that everything has to be open-sourced. I care about people being able to learn, build, and contribute, and open source is a powerful way to make that possible. But with very capable models, there are also questions about safety, misuse, and what happens once you release something you can’t take back.

That doesn’t mean I think every decision to keep a model closed is automatically right. You still have to ask: What could we share? How can researchers scrutinize these systems? How can people build on them? For me, that’s a real tension to keep working through, rather than something with a perfectly clean answer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a real tension there. Loving open source doesn’t necessarily mean believing every model should be released openly, regardless of its capabilities or risks. But it does mean taking transparency, access, and the ability for people to build on each other’s work seriously.

I can see reasons to be cautious about releasing powerful models. At the same time, I think those reasons should be explained clearly and questioned. Safety shouldn’t just become a blanket justification for keeping everything closed. For me, reconciling the two means holding on to those open-source values while being willing to debate where the boundaries should be.
